title: How to Clean Your Dryer Vent (Step by Step)
hook: Do your clothes take two cycles to dry, and does the laundry room feel hot and smell of burning? A clogged dryer vent wastes energy, and it is also a fire risk. In seven steps, you'll learn how to clear the lint safely, in about an hour. It is simple, but it matters, and what to do if it still dries slowly.
intro: Every load leaves lint, and not all of it stops in the trap. The rest travels through the duct to the outside, and slowly builds up. Lint is highly flammable, and a blocked vent traps heat. Cleaning it once a year is one of the most useful home maintenance jobs. Safety comes first. Always unplug the dryer before you start. If you have a gas dryer, or if you are not comfortable with the work, call a professional. Set aside an hour on a quiet weekend, and the job is easier than it sounds.
youNeedNarration: Here's what you need. A dryer vent brush kit, with flexible rods that attach to a drill. A vacuum cleaner with a hose attachment. A screwdriver or a nut driver for the clamps. Foil tape. Work gloves and a dust mask. And a flashlight. A helper can make moving the dryer much easier. Lay a towel on the floor. A helper makes the whole job quicker and safer.
heroImagePrompt: A clogged lint-filled dryer vent duct being cleaned with a long flexible brush, laundry room, bright light, photorealistic, no text

steps.title: Unplug the dryer
steps.narration: Step one. Turn off the dryer and unplug it from the wall. If you have a gas dryer, also turn off the gas valve, and do not disconnect the gas line yourself. If you're not sure about your type of dryer, call a professional. Let the dryer cool for at least thirty minutes if you recently used it. Clear the area around it, put on gloves and a dust mask, and open a window for ventilation. Never skip this, since it is the most important safety step in the whole job.
steps.tip: Unplug first, and gas dryers need a pro
steps.imagePrompt: A hand pulling a dryer power plug from a wall outlet in a laundry room, photorealistic, no text

steps.title: Pull the dryer out carefully
steps.narration: Step two. Slowly slide the dryer away from the wall, just far enough to reach the back. Ask someone to help, and protect the floor with a towel or cardboard. Watch the vent hose and the power cord as you move it. Don't stretch or crush them, and make sure that a gas dryer's flexible line does not kink. If there's too little space, leave the dryer where it is, and clean the duct from the outside. Ask your landlord or building manager first if you rent, because some buildings arrange this service for tenants.
steps.tip: Move slowly and protect the floor
steps.mistake: Crushing the duct against the wall
steps.imagePrompt: Two people sliding a dryer away from a laundry room wall, floor protected with cardboard, photorealistic, no text

steps.title: Disconnect the duct
steps.narration: Step three. Find the vent duct connecting the back of the dryer to the wall. It's held by metal clamps or foil tape. Loosen the clamps with a screwdriver, or peel off the tape, and gently pull the duct free from the dryer and the wall. Look inside. If it's packed with lint, you're in the right place. Check the duct for holes, crushing, or damage, and if it's plastic or foil, plan to replace it with metal. Tighten the clamps again after you clean, so no lint escapes into the room, and the joint stays sealed.
steps.mistake: Tearing the duct off by force
steps.imagePrompt: A hand loosening a metal clamp on a silver dryer vent duct behind a dryer with a screwdriver, photorealistic, no text

steps.title: Clean the duct
steps.narration: Step four. Attach the brush to the flexible rod, and connect it to a drill. Feed it into the duct, running the drill slowly in a clockwise direction, and add more rods as you go. Pull the brush back and forth to loosen the lint. Then use the vacuum hose to remove what's come out. Do this from both ends, inside and outside, if you can. Repeat until no more lint comes out. Wear a dust mask throughout. If the duct is long, more than thirty feet or ten metres, or has several bends, consider hiring a professional.
steps.imagePrompt: A long flexible brush attached to a drill being pushed into a dryer vent duct, lint falling, photorealistic, no text

steps.title: Clean the outside vent hood
steps.narration: Step five. Go outside, and find the vent hood on the wall. Check that the flap opens freely. Remove any lint, leaves, bird nests or debris blocking it, wearing gloves. If you see a screen or mesh covering the opening, remove it, because it clogs with lint and shouldn't be there. Clean the hood with a brush and a damp cloth. Run the dryer for a few seconds, and confirm that air flows out strongly. If it's weak, there is still a blockage. Keep bushes and snow away from the outside vent, since anything covering it will cut airflow right away.
steps.mistake: Covering the outlet with a mesh screen
steps.imagePrompt: An exterior wall dryer vent hood with the flap open and lint being removed by a gloved hand, photorealistic, no text

steps.title: Clean the lint trap and housing
steps.narration: Step six. Pull out the lint screen inside the dryer door, and remove all lint by hand. Wash it with warm soapy water and a soft brush every few months, as fabric softener leaves a film that blocks airflow. Let it dry completely. Use the vacuum's narrow attachment to clean the slot where the trap sits, and the back of the dryer where the duct connects. Clean the lint screen after every load as a habit. Signs of a clogged vent include clothes that stay damp, a hot dryer top, and a burning smell.
steps.tip: Wash the screen every few months
steps.mistake: Skipping the lint trap after each load
steps.imagePrompt: A hand removing a thick layer of grey lint from a dryer lint screen, photorealistic, no text

steps.title: Reconnect and test
steps.narration: Step seven. Reattach the duct to the dryer and the wall. Use a rigid or semi-rigid metal duct if possible, rather than foil or plastic, which can trap lint and catch fire. Keep the duct as short and straight as you can, and secure the joints with clamps or foil tape, not screws, which catch lint. Push the dryer back without crushing the duct, plug it in, and run it for a few minutes. Check outside for strong airflow. Make a note on your calendar for next year, and keep the brush kit somewhere handy.
steps.imagePrompt: A rigid metal dryer duct connected to the back of a dryer with foil tape and a clamp, photorealistic, no text

bonus.label: NOT WORKING?
bonus.title: If it still dries slowly
bonus.narration: If the dryer is still slow, look for the next cause. Check the outside flap, and make sure it opens fully when the dryer runs. Pour a little water on the lint screen. If it pools instead of soaking in, a film of softener is blocking the mesh, so scrub it. Look for sharp bends or a crushed duct behind the dryer. Do not overload the drum, because clothes need room to tumble.
bonus.tip: Water on the screen should soak in
bonus.imagePrompt: A hand holding a clean dryer lint screen over a sink while a small amount of water is poured onto the mesh, droplets visible. Photorealistic photograph for a home how-to video. Bright, tidy laundry room, soft daylight. Adult hands, no face visible. 16:9 landscape format. No text, no letters, no logos, no watermark.

bonus.label: CALL A PRO
bonus.title: When to call a professional
bonus.narration: Some vents are not a do-it-yourself job. If the duct runs a long way, through the roof, or inside a wall or ceiling, a professional has the right tools. The same goes for any gas dryer problem. If you smell gas, leave the house and call the gas company. If a burning smell returns after cleaning, unplug the dryer and have a technician check it.
bonus.imagePrompt: A service technician in work gloves kneeling behind a pulled-out dryer and inspecting the metal vent duct with a flashlight. Photorealistic photograph for a home how-to video. Bright, tidy laundry room, soft daylight. Adult hands, no face visible. 16:9 landscape format. No text, no letters, no logos, no watermark.

bonus.label: PREVENTION
bonus.title: Daily habits that prevent fires
bonus.narration: Small habits do most of the work. Empty the lint screen after every load, because it is the first place lint collects. Do not run the dryer when you are out of the house or asleep. Never dry items that contain gasoline, cooking oil or other flammable substances, because they can heat up on their own. Keep the area around the dryer clear of clutter, and keep a working smoke alarm nearby.
bonus.tip: Empty the lint screen every load
bonus.imagePrompt: A hand pulling a gray layer of lint off the lint screen of an open dryer, a tidy laundry basket beside the machine. Photorealistic photograph for a home how-to video. Bright, tidy laundry room, soft daylight. Adult hands, no face visible. 16:9 landscape format. No text, no letters, no logos, no watermark.

mistakesToAvoid.narration: Here are the mistakes to avoid. First, working on a plugged-in or gas dryer without the right precautions. Always unplug, and call a pro for gas. Second, using a foil or plastic duct, or long, bendy runs, which collect lint and hold heat. And third, waiting too long. Clean the vent at least once a year, or sooner if drying takes longer than usual. If you notice a burning smell, stop using the dryer and investigate straight away. Treat any burning smell as a warning, and don't ignore it.
items: Working on a live or gas dryer

recap.narration: Let's recap. Unplug the dryer. Pull it out carefully. Disconnect the duct. Clean the duct with a brush and a vacuum. Clean the outside vent hood. Clean the lint trap and housing. And reconnect with a metal duct, then test the airflow. Seven steps, about an hour, and a dryer that dries faster and safer. Bonus sections cover what to check if drying is still slow, when to call a professional, and the daily habits that prevent dryer fires.
items: Clean the lint trap and housing

outro: That's how you clean your dryer vent. If this saved you energy and gave you peace of mind, subscribe to WikiTube, because we publish a new how-to every single day. Tell us in the comments how much lint you found, and what you would like us to explain next. See you tomorrow. And clean your lint trap after every load, as a habit.

metadata.title: How to Clean Your Dryer Vent (Step by Step)
metadata.description:
Clothes taking too long to dry? In this step-by-step video you'll learn how to clean your dryer vent safely: unplug the dryer, pull it out carefully, disconnect the duct, clean it with a brush kit and a vacuum, clear the outside vent hood, clean the lint trap, then reconnect with a metal duct and test the airflow. A clogged vent wastes energy and can be a fire hazard, so do it once a year.

You'll need: a dryer vent brush kit, a vacuum with a hose, a screwdriver, foil tape and gloves, a flashlight.
